content: Nicotine nasal spray is a dependency agent approved by the FDA for smoking cessation. It is used to alleviate nicotine withdrawal symptoms. Common adverse reactions include skin irritation, nasal irritation, oral irritation, dizziness, headache, and insomnia. Adult Indications and Dosage Nicotine nasal spray is indicated as an aid for smoking cessation and should be used as part of a comprehensive behavioral smoking cessation program. The safety and efficacy of its use beyond six months have not been adequately studied and are not recommended. Dosage Instructions Patients must understand the proper use of nicotine nasal spray, including safe disposal of used containers. They should stop smoking completely when starting the therapy. Patients should not sniff, swallow, or inhale through the nose while administering the spray. The spray should be administered with the head tilted slightly back. Each dose consists of 1 mg of nicotine (2 sprays, one in each nostril). Patients typically start with 1 or 2 doses per hour, with a maximum of 40 mg (80 sprays) per day. For optimal results, patients should use at least 8 doses per day, as lower usage is less effective. Clinical trials show that patients who successfully quit smoking used the spray heavily during peak withdrawal periods, sometimes up to the maximum recommended dose. No specific tapering strategy has been proven optimal. Many patients simply stopped using the spray at their last clinic visit. Recommended discontinuation strategies include reducing the dose to one spray, using the spray less frequently, keeping a tally of daily usage, setting a steadily reducing usage target, skipping doses, or setting a planned quit date. The success of smoking cessation is influenced by the quality, intensity, and frequency of supportive care. Patients are more likely to quit smoking if they are seen frequently and participate in formal smoking cessation programs. The goal of nicotine nasal spray therapy is complete abstinence. If a patient cannot stop smoking by the fourth week of therapy, treatment should likely be discontinued. Patients who fail to quit may benefit from additional interventions and should be counseled before attempting to quit again under more favorable conditions. Contraindications Nicotine nasal spray is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity or allergy to nicotine or any component of the product. Warnings Nicotine, regardless of its source, is toxic and addictive. Smoking causes lung disease, cancer, and heart disease, and may adversely affect pregnant women or the fetus. The risks of nicotine replacement therapy should be weighed against the hazards of continued smoking and the likelihood of achieving smoking cessation without nicotine replacement. Pregnancy Nicotine nasal spray is classified as Pregnancy Category D. Tobacco smoke, which contains nicotine, hydrogen cyanide, and carbon monoxide, is harmful to the fetus. Nicotine has been shown in animal studies to cause fetal harm. Pregnant smokers should attempt cessation using educational and behavioral interventions before considering pharmacological approaches. If nicotine nasal spray is used during pregnancy, the patient should be informed of the potential risks to the fetus. Safety Note for Children Nicotine amounts tolerated by adult smokers can be toxic or fatal if used or ingested by children or pets. A full bottle of nicotine nasal spray contains 100 mg of nicotine, which remains even after the bottle is discarded. Patients should keep both used and unused containers out of reach of children and pets. Precautions Patients should stop smoking completely when initiating nicotine nasal spray therapy. Continuing to smoke while using the product may result in adverse effects due to higher peak nicotine levels than from smoking alone. Asthma and Reactive Airway Disease Exacerbation of bronchospasm has been reported in patients with pre-existing asthma. Nicotine nasal spray is not recommended for patients with severe reactive airway disease. Cardiovascular and Peripheral Vascular Diseases The risks of nicotine replacement therapy in patients with cardiovascular and peripheral vascular diseases should be carefully evaluated. Nicotine nasal spray should generally not be used during the immediate post-myocardial infarction period, in patients with serious arrhythmias, or in those with severe or worsening angina. Renal or Hepatic Impairment Nicotine is extensively metabolized, and its clearance depends on liver blood flow. Hepatic impairment may reduce clearance, and severe renal impairment may affect the clearance of nicotine or its metabolites. Endocrine Diseases Nicotine nasal spray should be used cautiously in patients with hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, or insulin-dependent diabetes, as nicotine stimulates catecholamine release. Peptic Ulcer Disease Nicotine delays healing in peptic ulcer disease. Nicotine nasal spray should be used cautiously in patients with active peptic ulcers and only when the benefits outweigh the risks. Accelerated Hypertension Nicotine therapy poses a risk for malignant hypertension in patients with accelerated hypertension. Use should be cautious and only when the benefits outweigh the risks. Adverse Reactions Adverse events reported during clinical trials include nasal irritation, runny nose, throat irritation, sneezing, and coughing. Nasal irritation was reported by nearly all patients during the first two days of treatment, with frequency and severity declining over time. Other common side effects include chest tightness, dyspepsia, paresthesia, constipation, and stomatitis. Overdosage The oral minimum acute lethal dose of nicotine in adult humans is reported to be 40 to 60 mg. A full bottle of nicotine nasal spray contains 100 mg of nicotine. Signs of nicotine toxicity include pallor, cold sweat, nausea, salivation, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, tremor, mental confusion, and weakness. Severe overdoses may result in prostration, hypotension, respiratory failure, convulsions, and death. Management of nicotine poisoning includes supportive measures such as diazepam or barbiturates for seizures, atropine for excessive bronchial secretions or diarrhea, respiratory support for respiratory failure, and vigorous fluid support for hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. Pharmacology Nicotine binds to nicotinic-cholinergic receptors in the autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla, neuromuscular junctions, and brain. It exerts stimulating effects in the cortex via the locus ceruleus and reward effects in the limbic system. At low doses, stimulant effects predominate, while at high doses, reward effects are more pronounced.
